BXL-2425-00016-v1.headline: Cut the parliament's own running budget by 5% for one month — a pay-cut signal to politicians — after nine months without a Brussels government.
BXL-2425-00016-v1.proposed_by: Françoise De Smedt (PTB) and Jan Busselen (PVDA/PTB)
BXL-2425-00016-v1.source_brief:
Brussels has been without a fully empowered government since the June 2024 elections — for more than nine months at the time of this vote. The Region is operating on provisional credits while running a structural deficit of over 1.6 billion euros, and parliament has been urged from multiple sides to show it grasps the gravity. This amendment targets the operating subsidy that finances the parliament itself, cutting it for April 2025 in a way that would constrain deputies' take-home pay.

- **What the amendment does:** It lowers the parliament's budget allocation (allocation de base 34.100.10, mission 34 Chancellerie) from 17,250 to 16,603.50 thousand euros for April 2025 — approximately a 5% reduction — and adjusts the totals in Article 6 and Annex 1 accordingly.
- **The context:** Multiple speakers noted that Brussels deputies earn roughly 5% more than their counterparts at the Federal Parliament and other Belgian assemblies. Supporters say reducing the subsidy would force the parliament's Bureau to translate that into lower remuneration, saving an estimated 600,000 euros a year if applied year-round.
- **A rival proposal:** another group announced simultaneously that it had tabled a separate, more drastic text — scheduled for the parliamentary Bureau on 2 April — proposing a 40% pay cut for deputies and ministers for as long as the government-formation deadlock lasts; they abstained on this amendment, calling it technically flawed and insufficient.
- **The rub:** Supporters argue it is symbolic but concrete accountability: elected officials should not earn more than federal colleagues while the Region drifts without a government. Opponents and abstainers counter that cutting a dotation does not automatically reduce salaries — the Bureau must still decide — and that the reduction covers only three months, making the headline saving figure approximate and the symbolic gesture hollow.
deep_facts: Amendment nr. 1 was tabled by Mme Françoise De Smedt and M. Jan Busselen (PTB/PVDA) to Article 6 (tableaux budgétaires) of A-86, the projet d'ordonnance de finances ouvrant des crédits provisoires pour les mois d'avril, mai et juin 2025 sur le budget de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

The amendment cuts allocation de base 34.100.10 (subventions de fonctionnement non neutralisées en SEC au sein de la RBC, mission 34 Chancellerie, programme 100 'Financer le Parlement de la RBC') from 17,250 to 16,603.50 thousand euros in both liquidation and engagement credits; the April 2025 provisional-credits column drops correspondingly from 34,500 to 33,853.50 thousand euros (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

In plenary debate, Stijn Bex (Groen) stated that Brussels deputies earn roughly 5% more than their counterparts at the Kamer, the Flemish Parliament and other Belgian assemblies, and argued that the Bureau could simply decide to align remuneration — saving an estimated 600,000 euros per year (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

PVDA/PTB tabled the amendment citing the Region's severe fiscal situation: a structural deficit exceeding 1.6 billion euros, provisional budgets instead of a proper annual budget, and a hiring freeze already in place; they invited all groups to support the amendment as a signal of collective accountability (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).
DéFI (Jonathan de Patoul) announced his group would vote in favour, saying it was a just and responsible measure that DéFI had defended before (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

Les Engagés (Alain Deneef) abstained, arguing that reducing the dotation does not automatically reduce salaries — a Bureau decision is still required — that the amendment covers only the first quarter rather than the period under discussion, and that the stated 650,000-euro saving figure was approximate and poorly justified; they pointed to their own separate text, scheduled for the Bureau on 2 April 2025, which would immediately reduce deputies' and ministers' salaries by 40% for the duration of the government-formation deadlock (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

N-VA (Gilles Verstraeten) stated before the amendment was formally tabled that he did not believe parliamentary salaries could be reduced by a budget amendment — it was a matter for the Bureau élargi — and that any salary comparison should be comprehensive and Belgium-wide before adjustments are made (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

The caretaker government had been in office since the June 2024 elections; at the time of the vote, Les Engagés characterised Brussels as having been 'sans gouvernement depuis plus de neuf mois', making it a prolonged constitutional and budgetary impasse (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

A separate issue was flagged in the same debate: Standard & Poor's was expected to deliver a credit-rating verdict on Brussels in June 2025, and the caretaker Finance Minister Gatz warned that the Region's fiscal trajectory was under close scrutiny (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).
BXL-2425-00016-v1.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The mechanism chosen — cutting the parliamentary dotation rather than mandating a direct pay reduction — reveals the legal constraint: parliament cannot legislate its own members' salaries by ordinary budget amendment; only the Bureau can. So the amendment is, in effect, a pressure move rather than a direct executive act, which is exactly what Les Engagés attacked as amateurish while proposing the same idea through the only vehicle (the Bureau) that could actually deliver it.
- The split between PTB's 5% cut and Les Engagés' 40% cut reflects two different political calculations: PTB's figure aligns Brussels deputies with other Belgian assemblies (framed as fairness, not punishment), while 40% is explicitly framed as coercive — a penalty designed to force parties to the government-formation table.
- DéFI and Groen supporting the amendment, and Les Engagés abstaining rather than voting against, signals that no group wanted to be seen defending the status quo salary premium during a fiscal emergency — the disagreement is entirely about the right instrument and the right cut, not about the principle.
- The coexistence of a 1.6-billion-euro structural deficit and a 5% pay premium for deputies is a politically combustible combination; whatever the legal route, the trajectory of the debate points toward a Bureau decision aligning Brussels salaries with the federal level, making the amendment's defeat less a rejection of the idea than a deferral.
BXL-2425-00016-v1.raw_fr: L'amendement n° 1 réduit d'environ 5 % la subvention de fonctionnement inscrite à l'allocation de base 34.100.10 (mission 34, programme 100 'Financer le Parlement de la RBC') pour les crédits provisoires d'avril 2025, avec les ajustements correspondants à l'article 6 et à l'annexe 1. Le débat s'inscrit dans le contexte d'un blocage institutionnel de plus de neuf mois sans gouvernement de plein exercice et d'un déficit structurel régional dépassant 1,6 milliard d'euros.

BXL-2425-00016-v5.headline: Fix the law so older diesel and petrol cars can keep driving into Brussels until the end of 2026, repairing the botched wording of the earlier Low Emission Zone delay.
BXL-2425-00016-v5.proposed_by: Jamal Ikazban (PS), Anne-Charlotte d'Ursel (MR), Mounir Laarissi, Ibrahim Dönmez, Sofia Bennani, Imane Belguenani, Clémentine Barzin
BXL-2425-00016-v5.source_brief:
In October 2024 the Brussels Parliament passed an ordinance (A-10) postponing the next phase of the Low Emission Zone — which would have banned Euro 5 diesel and Euro 2 vehicles from 2025 — by two years to 1 January 2027. The Conseil d'État subsequently identified a legal defect in the wording: the text did not explicitly state that vehicles already authorised to circulate would continue to be so, and it did not include the compensating measures required under the constitutional standstill obligation on environmental protection. This proposition d'ordonnance (A-79) is a corrective rewrite of article 3.2.16 §6 of the Brussels Air, Climate and Energy Code, replacing the October 2024 wording with a version the Conseil d'État considers compliant, with retroactive effect from 1 January 2025.

- **What it changes:** The text restores legal certainty for more than 30,000 Brussels-registered vehicles and 8,000 light utility vehicles — plus over 700,000 vehicles nationally — that would have been banned under the original 2025 deadline.
- **The compensating measures:** To satisfy the standstill condition, the text is accompanied by commitments including mobile enforcement teams to check foreign vehicles, anti-particle-filter-fraud detection, remote emissions sensing, and expansion of electric-vehicle charging infrastructure.
- **Why again:** An amendment adopted in committee adds an explicit clause confirming that vehicles already permitted to enter the LEZ retain that right — the specific fix the Conseil d'État requested to avoid interpretation disputes.
- **The rub:** Supporters say the postponement is a socially just transition measure in a difficult economic climate, that Brussels already meets all European air-quality norms, and that buildings (responsible for 60-75% of Brussels air pollution) are the bigger lever. Opponents argue that every LEZ delay chips away at the credibility of the phasing schedule, penalises the tens of thousands who already sold compliant vehicles in anticipation of the rule, and risks eroding the flexibility needed for the 2028, 2030 and 2036 milestones.
deep_facts: The proposition d'ordonnance (dossier A-79/1, 2, 3 et 4 – 2024/2025) amends the ordonnance du 2 mai 2013 portant le Code bruxellois de l'Air, du Climat et de la Maîtrise de l'Énergie (Cobrace) by replacing article 3.2.16 §6 with a corrected formulation, with retroactive effect from 1 January 2025 (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

The first postponement ordinance (A-10, adopted 17 October 2024) had delayed the LEZ phase banning Euro 5 diesel and Euro 2 vehicles from 1 January 2025 to 1 January 2027; A-79 corrects its wording without reopening the date (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

The Conseil d'État (avis numéro 77.511/1, on a five-day referral from parliament and a 30-day referral from the Environment Minister) found that the wording of A-10 was not fully compliant with the constitutional standstill obligation under Article 23 of the Constitution and recommended two additions: explicit confirmation that already-authorised vehicles remain authorised, and a description of compensating measures to offset any air-quality regression (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

A MR amendment adopted in committee adds the explicit clause that vehicles already authorised to circulate within the LEZ will continue to be so — the specific textual fix requested by the Conseil d'État to prevent interpretation disputes (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

Figures cited in debate: without the postponement, the 2025 deadline would have banned more than 30,000 Brussels-registered vehicles and more than 8,000 Brussels-registered light utility vehicles, as well as more than 700,000 vehicles nationally seeking to enter the zone (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

Proposers cited Brussels Environnement data confirming that the Region has met all European air-quality norms since 2022 — including PM10, PM2.5 and nitrogen oxides — and is already below its 2030 targets for several pollutants; Environment Minister Maron confirmed in the 12 March 2025 committee meeting that a two-year delay would not prevent the Region from meeting its climate objectives (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

Compensating measures accompanying the postponement include: enhanced LEZ-enforcement conditions, mobile teams to control foreign vehicles, detection of particle-filter fraud, real-emissions evaluation via remote sensing, and expansion of public electric-vehicle charging infrastructure (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

Ikazban (PS) emphasised that buildings account for 60 to 75% of Brussels air pollution while road transport represents only 25%, arguing the LEZ cannot be the sole lever for air-quality improvement; the postponement is explicitly framed as a social-accompaniment measure, not an abandonment of the broader LEZ schedule (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

PTB (Oliver Rittweger de Moor) voted against both A-10 in October 2024 and A-79 in March 2025, arguing that the LEZ cannot be justified without genuine public-transport alternatives; they noted STIB fares had risen 10% over six months and service had been cut on dozens of bus lines (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).

The 2028, 2030 and 2036 LEZ access restrictions and the Region's carbon-neutrality and greenhouse-gas-reduction targets remain unchanged; proposers repeated this commitment explicitly to reassure environmental groups and the Environment Minister (CRI, 21 Mar 2025).
BXL-2425-00016-v5.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- A-79 is structurally a clean-up bill: the political decision to postpone was taken in October 2024; this text is about making that decision legally watertight. That dynamic matters — a party that opposed the postponement on principle when A-10 was voted could still accept the technical fix without reversing course, producing an unusually broad majority.
- The Conseil d'État's requirement to describe compensating measures is the substantive upgrade in A-79 over A-10: it forces the legislature to put on record what it intends to do to protect air quality during the extra two years, creating a traceable commitment that environmental groups can hold up against the 2028 milestone debate.
- The 60-75% buildings / 25% transport framing, repeated by multiple proposers, is doing political work beyond the immediate text: it pre-positions the next fiscal battle over building-renovation budgets as the primary air-quality lever, potentially softening future resistance to further LEZ flexibility if building-renovation funding is secured.
- The Flemish LEZ postponement — mentioned as a source of citizen confusion if Brussels had held to its original schedule — shows how cross-regional policy divergence is now a political argument for regional alignment downward, a precedent that could resurface in future LEZ debates at the 2028 deadline.
BXL-2425-00016-v5.raw_fr: La proposition d'ordonnance (A-79) remplace l'article 3.2.16 §6 du Cobrace par une formulation conforme aux exigences du Conseil d'État (avis 77.511/1), avec effet rétroactif au 1er janvier 2025. Elle consolide juridiquement le report au 1er janvier 2027 de la phase LEZ excluant les véhicules diesel Euro 5 et Euro 2, décidé par l'ordonnance du 17 octobre 2024, en ajoutant explicitement que les véhicules déjà autorisés à circuler conservent ce droit et en détaillant les mesures compensatoires exigées par le principe de standstill constitutionnel. Les échéances LEZ de 2028, 2030 et 2036 demeurent inchangées.
